c.tagline: A coastal gateway to Seoraksan National Park, with East Sea beaches and Korea's famous soft tofu cuisine

card: Very widely accepted, including small shops; cash rarely needed

taxi.fare: Metered, roughly ₩4,800 base fare plus per-km rate
taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard and reliable; Kakao T makes ordering easy without much Korean

emergency.note: 112 for police, 119 for medical/fire emergencies; English-language support is available on both lines

walk: Central Sokcho and the beach areas are walkable; Seoraksan National Park requires a bus or car

safety.safety: Very safe city with low crime, popular with domestic and international tourists alike
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare even in crowded markets

hood_landmark.Sokcho Beach: Sokcho Beach's Expo Tower and boardwalk
hood_landmark.Abai Village: Abai Village's famous sundae sausage alley
hood_landmark.Seoraksan Entrance (Soraksan-dong): The cable car base station into Seoraksan National Park
hood_landmark.Daepo-dong (Harbor): Daepo Harbor's sea fountain and beach cable car
hood_landmark.Sokcho Central Market: Sokcho Jungang Market's fresh and dried seafood stalls

hood_desc: The main city beach lined with cafes and the iconic Expo Tower, popular for sunrise views over the East Sea.
A distinctive community founded by North Korean refugees, reached by a hand-pulled ferry, now known for its signature blood-sausage dish.
The gateway to Seoraksan National Park's cable car and hiking trails, lined with motels and restaurants for hikers.
The working harbor area with a sea fountain, cable car, and fresh catch restaurants.
A historic covered market dating to 1953, the best place for fresh seafood and local street food.
lodging: Sokcho Good Morning Hotel and Resort

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though most Koreans prefer bottled or filtered.

transit.sys: Sokcho city bus network, including routes to Seoraksan National Park
transit.pay: T-money rechargeable transit card or cash
transit.note: Buses run regularly from downtown to the Seoraksan cable car base

transport.air: Yangyang International Airport (YNY), about 30 min away, with limited domestic and some international flights
transport.train: KTX-Eumseong high-speed rail line connects Seoul to nearby Gangneung/Sokcho area stations
transport.bus: Frequent intercity buses connect Sokcho to Seoul (about 2-2.5 hr)
transport.car: Well connected via the Seoul-Yangyang Expressway

net.m: Excellent 5G/4G coverage nationwide, among the fastest in the world
net.w: Free wifi widely available in cafes, hotels, and public areas
net.ap: An SK Telecom, KT, or LG U+ tourist SIM or eSIM, or a portable wifi egg rental

tip.s: Not customary; tipping can even cause confusion
tip.r: Not expected; service charge is never added at typical restaurants

landmarks: Seoraksan National Park
South Korea's most celebrated national park at Sokcho's doorstep, a UNESCO biosphere of granite pinnacles, waterfalls and blazing autumn foliage.
Ulsanbawi Rock
A jagged six-peaked granite ridge reached by a stairway of 800-plus steps, rewarding climbers with Seoraksan's most dramatic panorama.
Sinheungsa Temple and Great Unification Buddha
An ancient temple at the park entrance guarded by a 14.6-metre gilt-bronze seated Buddha praying for Korean reunification.
Seorak Cable Car and Gwongeumseong Fortress
A scenic cable-car ride to a ruined mountain fortress ledge with effortless views over Sokcho, the sea and a sea of peaks.
Abai Village
A nostalgic neighbourhood founded by North Korean refugees, famous for stuffed squid sundae and the hand-pulled getbae ferry across the harbour channel.
Sokcho Tourist and Fishermen's Market (Jungang Market)
The city's bustling central market, a food-lover's maze famed for dakgangjeong sweet-crispy chicken and fresh East Sea seafood.
Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion
A seaside pavilion on the rocks at the harbour mouth, linked by footbridge and beloved as Sokcho's sunrise viewpoint.
Cheongchoho Lake and Expo Tower
A tranquil lagoon in the city centre ringed by a promenade and overlooked by the sail-shaped 1999 Expo observation tower.
Sokcho Beach
A broad white-sand city beach steps from the express bus terminal, packed with parasols in summer and photogenic pine groves year-round.
Naksansa Temple
A 1,300-year-old seaside temple south of Sokcho where the towering Haesugwaneum statue of the Goddess of Mercy gazes over the East Sea.

train.note: Sokcho currently has no railway station at all - the old Donghae Bukbu line to the north was severed by the division of the peninsula and never rebuilt. The usual rail approach is Korail's KTX-Isan from Seoul Cheongnyangni to Gangneung in about two hours (https://www.korail.com/), then a bus of roughly an hour up the coast. The East Sea Northern Line from Seoul to Sokcho is under construction with an opening targeted around 2027, which would cut the journey to about 1 hr 40 min. No international trains run from South Korea.

bus.note: Two terminals about 3 km apart serve the town: the Express Bus Terminal in the south near Daepohang and the Intercity Bus Terminal in the north. Buses leave the Seoul Express Bus Terminal roughly every 30 minutes for the 2.5-3 hr run over the Misiryeong pass for around 15,000 won, with intercity services to Chuncheon (about 2 hrs) and Gangneung (about 1 hr). Book express departures at Kobus (https://www.kobus.co.kr/) and intercity ones at Bustago (https://www.bustago.or.kr/), or buy at the terminal kiosks. South Korea runs no international coaches.

ferry.note: Sokcho's International Passenger Terminal was built for sailings to Zarubino near Vladivostok and on to Hunchun in China, but that route has been dormant for years and nothing is currently scheduled, so the terminal handles no regular passenger traffic. What remains are local fishing and sightseeing boats from Dongmyeonghang and Daepohang, plus the hand-pulled Gaetbae raft that ferries people across the narrow Cheongchoho inlet to Abai village for a token fare. Anyone wanting a sea crossing has to travel to Donghae or Busan.
